351.history: The long spit on the Abhainn uaine, a short hour's walk under Doire mhòr, held its foreshore in common, and A' Chompanaidh's first surveyors found it covered with their own men. A' Chompanaidh built its coal quay there, and for a century barges loaded the hill's coal for the coast. On the first day of the rising the crews took the quay and sank two loaded barges across its mouth; the boatman Pàdraig Reamhar knocked the plugs from a hull he had built with his own father. No coal left the hills by water again in the age. Its pilots guided A' Chompanaidh's barges through the shoals below the spit for a century, and the rivalry with Inis ìseal downstream went on untouched by all of it.
351.known_for: the barges sunk across its quay

422.history: The red hill-fort of the east sent Fionnghal nic Artair to Cathair dhearg in the early years, and hers is the only defence of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig that survives from the time it went out; the council filed her letter. The city kept its own counsel through the age. In the war its custodians sent grain south and read their declaration from the steps of the hall, quoting her sentence a hundred and twenty-seven years after she wrote it. The mills of Muileann dhomhain ground its bread and its custodians sent grain west to the camps in the hunger years by the old custom, asking nothing for it.
422.known_for: Fionnghal's letter, read again in the war

132.history: The walled harbour of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig heard Murchadh Seabhag preach the hawk's old freedom against the strangers' tithe, and a century later Ìomhar Seabhag's sermons went out from it in copies to the camps and the burial clubs. The hawk-shrines opened again along its bay in the season the fever returned. Its fishing families were proud to the end of the age of having chased A' Chompanaidh's first customs men off their harbour. Murchadh Seabhag preached from the steps of its temple, and copies of his sermons were carried inland to the camps by fishermen. Its harbour was shut to A' Chompanaidh's shipping in the war.

297.history: The long walled city of the south follows Macha, and its oak woods had been cut for A' Chompanaidh's pit-props since the first contracts. The age's rolls note the day the last oak of its own cutting came down, and the priests of Macha who would not stand for the blessing of the coin were many of them its people. Its priests of Macha were the first to refuse to stand for the blessing of the humans' coin in the capital's temple, and many of them followed the dissenters to the forest.
297.known_for: the oaks that went for pit-props

23.history: The great city below the old ruin refused the mark when it was first made law, and went on paying in kind at its market for a season after the rest of the country had given in. Am Fiabhras Glas came to it in the high summer of the hundred and thirty-eighth year, and for the first time in the town's memory the market shut, stall by stall; the longest list of dead in the roll was the street of the carters. It keeps below its walls the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, and the market that refused the coin gave way at last only when A' Chompanaidh's tool-sellers would not cross its bridge for anything else.

77.history: The great hill city of the north-east kept the last hall of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, and Samuel Wren spent a winter there learning what the masters would teach a stranger. Its master Aonghas mac Coinnich put to his students the question why the humans cannot see the colour in broken coal that every Dia-thìreach child sees, and did not answer it; a generation later George Tolley shut the hall over a lecture on whether that blindness was a kind of sickness, and Seònaid nic Dhùghaill was the last of its masters to teach openly. Am Fiabhras Glas came to it at the dark of a later year, and killed the physician Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had sent. The school's last masters went on teaching under the trees of Flidais after the hall was shut, and their pupils carried the disputations to Inis bhàn.
77.known_for: the shut hall of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean
